newsitem.title: HONG KONG: PRESS DIGEST-Hong Kong Newspaper Headlines-Dec 23.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-Hong Kong Newspaper Headlines-Dec 23.

text.p: These are some of the leading stories in the Hong Kong press on Monday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

-- TA KUNG PAO -- The provisional legislature has been acknowledged by people from all walks of life in Hong Kong, who believed that the Chief Executive would lead Hong Kong people to realise "Hong Kong people ruling Hong Kong."

-- Young people in Beijing are celebrating Christmas, which used to a festival of western expatriates only. A Christmas tree costs 300 yuan, the average monthly salary of a worker. The buyers are mostly fashionable young people in their early 30's.

-- HONG KONG DAILY NEWS -- Some members of the United Front Against the Provisional Legislature said the Hong Kong police were trying to please Beijing by limitnng their demonstrations and prosecuting them.

-- MING PAO -- Chief Executive-designate Tung Chee-hwa would meet Governor Chris Patten for the first time since his selection this afternoon. Tung said he would try to change Patten's attitude towards the provisional legislature.
-- Research showed that Shanghainese consume 3,000 metric tonnes of snake meat and export 70 tonnes every year, causing pressure on snake resources in the area.

-- SOUTH CHINA MORNING POST -- Dai-Ichi Securities' managing director in Hong Kong said that once the handover was safely out of the way, Japanese investors would rush to Hong Kong to escape stiflingly low yields at home.
-- The 108-storey Nina Tower, potentially Asia's tallest building, was believed to be back on track for construction once more following months of delay over height restriction problems.

-- HONGKONG STANDARD -- Chinese Vice Premier Zhu Rongji prodicted that inflation would not rebound next year despite strong economic growth, and said that social stability was essential in the key year of 1997.
-- The United States Congress would consider a number of major statutory changes to trade controls with China next year.
